1) the immune response to Mtb infection in humans is mediated by CD4 T cells and CD8 T cell subsets; 2) the balance between the different functional signatures of these cells is important in determining the outcome of infection, i.e., the progression to active or latent disease; 3) the immune response in TB disease is characterized by a Th1 profile of CD4 T cells; 4) the immune response of latent TB infection is characterized by a multifunctional CD
CD4 and CD 8 T cell responses to Mtb are characterized by different functional profiles that are associated with protection or disease.

(1) the immune response in active TB patients is characterized by an increased frequency of CD4+ and CD8+ T cell clones with a multifunctional profile, (2) CD4+ and/or CD8+ T helper 1 cells with a multifunction profile are associated to the control of Mtb infection in subjects with latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) and (3) CD4+ Th17 cells are associated to disease activity in LTBI subjects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of T cell subsets and their effector functions in human tuberculosis (TB) and the role of these cells in controlling the infection.
understanding the immune response to TB in order to identify new targets for the diagnosis and treatment of the infection and the disease.

the study of T cells in human tuberculosis, with the aim to better characterize the immune response to the pathogen and the host immune response to vaccination, in order to improve diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic tools.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, although the role of T cells in TB has been largely studied, the role of different subsets of CD4 and in particular CD8 cells in the immune response against Mtb is still unclear.
, although there are many aspects that are not yet fully understood, there is a clear indication that a polyfunctional T cell profile is associated with protection in Mtb infection.
the role of T cells in TB infection is not yet fully understood, and further studies are required to elucidate the mechanisms that underlie the immune response in TB.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the functional signature of the T cell response in human TB infection is a promising tool for the identification of biomarkers that can be used in diagnosis and prognosis, as well as to monitor the response to treatment and vaccination.
the functional signatures of T cells subsets in human TB, will be a good marker to monitor the disease and the immune response in TB infected individuals.
CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses are important for protection against Mtb infection and disease and that these responses can be measured in peripheral blood of infected individuals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the functional signature of CD4 and/or CD8 T cells may be a good tool to discriminate between subjects with latent infection and subjects with active disease.

the study of the immune response toward TB is a complex issue and that the knowledge of the immune system is crucial to understand how the immune response can be used to improve the outcome of this infection.
